title: #你的模型并不等于系统：构建面向生产环境 AI 的 MLOps 反馈闭环
author: SotaTek | AI & Blockchain Innovation Partner
content:
A machine learning model can achieve excellent evaluation results and still fail in production.

The model hasn't changed. The code hasn't changed. The deployment is healthy.

But prediction quality is declining.

Maybe the input distribution has shifted. Maybe an upstream data pipeline changed its schema. Maybe the business environment has evolved. Or, in a generative AI application, the model provider updated its API, a prompt changed, or a retrieval pipeline started returning different context.

This is why deploying a model is not the same as operating an AI system.

At SotaTek, we approach MLOps as a continuous engineering discipline: version what affects behavior, observe production signals, identify the source of degradation, and decide whether to fix the data, update the model, roll back, or redesign the system.

Let's look at what that actually requires.

1. MLOps Is More Than Model Monitoring

Model monitoring is one component of MLOps, not the entire operating model.

A production MLOps system needs to connect experimentation, data pipelines, model training, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, and incident response.

Capability Engineering responsibility
Experiment tracking Record datasets, parameters, metrics, and results
Model registry Manage approved model artifacts and versions
CI/CD Test and promote code and model changes
Continuous training Rebuild models when evidence justifies it
Data pipelines Maintain reliable training and inference inputs
Evaluation Validate candidate models against release criteria
Monitoring Detect abnormal production behavior
Observability Investigate why behavior changed
Rollback Restore a previously approved version

A dashboard might tell you that accuracy has dropped.

An operational MLOps system should help answer:

  • Which model version was running?
  • Did the input distribution change?
  • Was there a feature or schema issue?
  • Which deployment introduced the regression?
  • Is the degradation affecting business outcomes?
  • Should the team roll back, retrain, or fix the upstream pipeline?

The objective is not just to detect a problem. It's to make the next engineering action clear.

2. The Production Unit Is No Longer Just the Model

For conventional machine learning, teams often focus on the model artifact, features, training dataset, and inference environment.

Generative AI expands the operational surface.

A production LLM application may depend on:

  • Foundation-model and provider versions
  • System prompts and few-shot examples
  • Context-window composition
  • Embedding models
  • RAG retrieval and reranking configuration
  • Guardrails
  • Tool definitions
  • Agent workflows and permissions
  • Token consumption
  • Human escalation rules

Consider an enterprise support assistant.

Its behavior might change even if the application code remains untouched: 

Release 2.4.0
    |
    +-- LLM: model-v1
    +-- Prompt: support-v18
    +-- Embedding: embedding-v3
    +-- Reranker: reranker-v1
    +-- Retrieval top_k: 5
    +-- Guardrails: policy-v4

Release 2.4.1
    |
    +-- LLM: model-v2
    +-- Prompt: support-v18
    +-- Embedding: embedding-v3
    +-- Reranker: reranker-v2
    +-- Retrieval top_k: 8
    +-- Guardrails: policy-v4

Both releases may use the same application code, but they do not represent the same AI system.

If answer quality changes between these releases, the team needs enough metadata to identify which component contributed to the regression.

This is why modern AI operations must version more than model checkpoints.

3. Version Everything That Can Change Production Behavior

A reproducible release should capture the complete configuration required to understand and reproduce its behavior.

For conventional ML, track:

  • Dataset and feature versions
  • Model artifact
  • Hyperparameters
  • Runtime environment
  • Evaluation report
  • Deployment configuration

For LLM applications, also track:

  • Foundation-model version
  • System prompt version
  • Few-shot examples
  • Embedding model
  • Retrieval configuration
  • Reranker version
  • Guardrails
  • Tool schemas
  • Agent workflow configuration

A release manifest could look like this: 

release: support-agent-2.4.1

model:
  provider: approved-provider
  version: model-2026-09

prompt:
  version: support-system-v18

retrieval:
  embedding: embedding-v4
  reranker: reranker-v2
  top_k: 8

evaluation:
  groundedness: 0.976
  task_success: 0.943
  critical_failures: 0

deployment:
  previous_version: support-agent-2.4.0
  rollback_enabled: true

These values are illustrative configuration, not measured SotaTek performance data.

The important part is maintaining lineage between the release, its dependencies, and its evaluation results.

Without that lineage, regression analysis becomes guesswork.

4. Build an MLOps Lifecycle That Can Be Reproduced

A production ML lifecycle should make every transition explicit. 

Experiment
    |
    v
Code + Data + Parameters
    |
    v
Automated Training Pipeline
    |
    +-- Data Validation
    +-- Training
    +-- Evaluation
    |
    v
Model Registry
    |
    v
Release Gate
    |
    v
Staging
    |
    +-- Integration Tests
    +-- Performance Tests
    +-- Acceptance Tests
    |
    v
Production
    |
    v
Telemetry + Monitoring
    |
    v
Alert / Evaluation
    |
    +-------------------+
    |                   |
    v                   v
 Rollback          Retrain / Improve

CI validates code and configuration changes. CD promotes approved artifacts through deployment environments.

Continuous training (CT) can rebuild models when production evidence indicates that the existing model is no longer suitable.

But automatic retraining should not be the default response to every drift alert.

A distribution change is evidence that something changed. It does not prove that retraining will solve the problem.

5. Drift Detection Is Not the Same as Model Failure

One of the most important distinctions in production monitoring is understanding what actually changed.

There are several different failure signals.

Data quality issues

Inputs may contain missing values, invalid categories, unexpected timestamps, schema errors, or out-of-range values.

The data pipeline may be broken even when the underlying business distribution is stable.

Training-serving skew

The training and inference pipelines produce systematically different features.

For example, a feature may be calculated using one normalization rule during training and another during production.

Data drift

The statistical distribution of production inputs changes compared with the chosen baseline.

A credit model trained primarily on salaried employees may begin receiving a larger proportion of self-employed applicants.

Prediction drift

The distribution of model outputs changes.

A fraud model may suddenly classify more transactions as suspicious. That could indicate degradation, but it could also mean fraud activity has genuinely increased.

Concept drift

The relationship between inputs and outcomes changes.

Consumer purchasing patterns that previously predicted churn may stop working after a competitor changes its pricing strategy.

Feature distributions can remain relatively stable while model performance deteriorates.

These signals should not trigger the same automated response.

6. Build a Diagnostic Loop Before Triggering Retraining

A useful production response flow is: 

Drift Detected
      |
      v
Validate Data Quality
      |
      v
Measure Actual Model Impact
      |
      v
Root-Cause Analysis
      |
      +-- Data error --------> Fix Pipeline
      |
      +-- Temporary shift --> Continue Monitoring
      |
      +-- Model decay -------> Evaluate Retraining
      |
      +-- Structural shift --> Redesign Model

The key is to distinguish a change in input distribution from a change in actual model quality.

When ground-truth labels become available, compare predictions against real outcomes.

For a classification model, relevant metrics may include:

  • Accuracy
  • Precision
  • Recall
  • F1
  • Business-specific false-positive and false-negative rates

For regression, consider MAE or RMSE.

The evaluation metric should reflect the actual cost of model errors. A fraud detection system, for example, may care more about missed fraud than overall accuracy.

A drift alert is a reason to investigate, not an automatic instruction to retrain.

7. LLM Monitoring Needs Different Telemetry

Traditional ML monitoring focuses on data quality, prediction distributions, model performance, and infrastructure.

LLM applications need additional signals.

Layer Production signals
Model Answer correctness, refusal rate
Retrieval Recall\@K, relevance, reranker quality
Generation Groundedness, hallucination, citation accuracy
Performance Time to first token, end-to-end latency
Economics Input/output tokens, cost per request
Safety Guardrail violations, sensitive-data exposure
Workflow Human escalation, task completion

For RAG systems, retrieval and generation should be monitored separately.

If groundedness falls, there are at least two possible explanations:

  1. The correct evidence was never retrieved.
  2. The correct evidence reached the model, but the model failed to use it.

Those failures require different interventions.

A useful trace structure might look like: 

{
  "request_id": "req-8f32",
  "model_version": "model-v2",
  "prompt_version": "support-v18",
  "retrieval": {
    "embedding_version": "embedding-v4",
    "top_k": 8,
    "documents_retrieved": 8,
    "latency_ms": 145
  },
  "generation": {
    "input_tokens": 3200,
    "output_tokens": 420,
    "latency_ms": 1800
  },
  "evaluation": {
    "groundedness": 0.94,
    "citation_valid": true
  }
}

This is an illustrative telemetry schema. A production implementation should also apply data minimization, access controls, retention policies, and redaction for sensitive inputs and outputs.

The purpose of tracing is to reconstruct the execution path without exposing more user data than necessary.

8. AI Agents Need Trajectory Monitoring

For an AI agent, the final answer is only part of the execution.

An agent may retrieve information, select tools, invoke APIs, retry failed operations, request approval, and execute business actions.

Monitoring only the final response misses most of the operational behavior.

Consider this workflow: 

User Request
     |
     v
    Agent
     |
     +-- Retrieval
     |
     +-- Tool A
     |
     +-- Tool B
     |
     +-- Reason / Decide
     |
     v
Business Action
     |
     v
Final Response

Useful production signals include:

  • Task-success rate
  • Tool-selection accuracy
  • Invalid tool arguments
  • Number of tool calls
  • Permission violations
  • Looping behavior
  • Human-approval rate
  • Recovery after tool failure
  • Total latency
  • Cost per completed task

An agent that reaches the correct result after 25 unnecessary tool calls may be technically successful but operationally inefficient.

For many enterprise workflows, cost per successful task is more meaningful than cost per token.

More importantly, an agent that executes an unauthorized action must trigger a security response, not just a performance alert.

9. Monitoring Must Connect to Operational Actions

The strongest monitoring systems do not stop at generating alerts.

They connect production signals to a defined response. 

Production AI
      |
      v
Telemetry Layer
      |
      v
Monitoring / Evaluation
      |
      v
Threshold / Anomaly
      |
      v
Alerting
      |
      v
Incident Triage
      |
      +-- Observe
      |
      +-- Reduce Traffic
      |
      +-- Rollback
      |
      +-- Retrain
      |
      +-- Human Escalation
      |
      v
Re-evaluation
      |
      v
Controlled Release

Define baselines before alerts

A threshold has little meaning without a useful comparison point.

Depending on the metric, baselines may include:

  • Training data
  • Validation data
  • Previous production window
  • Previous model version
  • Control cohort
  • Historical seasonal period

A retailer comparing December traffic with October may see significant distribution changes that are simply seasonal behavior.

Monitoring design requires domain knowledge.

Avoid alert fatigue

Monitoring everything is not necessarily good monitoring.

Prioritize signals that correspond to meaningful business, reliability, or safety risks.

Alert Severity Response
High GPU utilization Low Capacity review
Data drift above threshold Medium Investigate
Model accuracy below SLA High Block next rollout
Sensitive-data exposure Critical Disable affected workflow
Unauthorized agent action Critical Stop agent and initiate incident response

Monitoring tells you that something is wrong. Observability helps you understand why.

Build rollback before you need it

A new model should rarely receive 100% of production traffic immediately when failures can materially affect customers or operations.

Common deployment strategies include:

  • Blue/green deployment
  • Canary release
  • Shadow deployment
  • Champion/challenger models
  • Feature flags
  • Previous-version rollback

A canary release exposes a small percentage of production traffic to a candidate model while comparing its quality, latency, errors, and business metrics with the incumbent.

10. Turn Production Incidents Into Regression Tests

Production failures should improve the next release.

A useful feedback loop is: 

Production Failure
       |
       v
Root Cause
       |
       v
New Evaluation Case
       |
       v
Fix
       |
       v
Regression Test
       |
       v
Release

For example, if an LLM assistant repeatedly cites outdated policy documents, add those scenarios to the evaluation suite.

If an agent attempts an unauthorized tool call, add a test that verifies the permission boundary.

Over time, the evaluation dataset becomes a record of what production has taught the engineering team.

This is why model evaluation and MLOps should be designed together rather than operated by disconnected teams.

11. Monitor Business Outcomes, Not Only Technical Health

An AI system can be technically healthy while failing commercially.

Imagine a support assistant with:

  • 97% groundedness
  • 99.9% uptime
  • Low infrastructure error rates

But employees ignore it because it adds two minutes to every workflow.

From an infrastructure perspective, the system looks healthy. From a business perspective, it is failing.

Connect AI telemetry to metrics such as:

  • Handling time
  • Automation rate
  • Defect reduction
  • Conversion
  • User adoption
  • Human-review workload
  • Cost per completed task
  • Revenue or cost impact

The goal is not to maximize model accuracy in isolation. It is to maintain a reliable system that delivers the expected business outcome.

12. A Practical Production MLOps Checklist

Before calling an AI system production-ready, verify:

Versioning and reproducibility

  • Models, prompts, datasets, and configurations are versioned.
  • Every deployment can be reproduced.
  • Approved model versions are tracked.

Evaluation and release

  • Release criteria are defined.
  • Candidate models are evaluated before promotion.
  • Regression tests cover known production failures.

Monitoring and observability

  • Production inference telemetry is collected.
  • Data quality and drift are monitored.
  • Model quality is measured when ground truth becomes available.
  • Latency, availability, and infrastructure are monitored.
  • Cost and resource consumption are visible.

Generative AI and agents

  • Retrieval and generation are monitored separately.
  • Prompt and model versions are traceable.
  • Agent tools, trajectories, permissions, and approvals are recorded.

Incident response

  • Alerts have defined response procedures.
  • Rollback is available.
  • Someone is explicitly accountable for production AI performance.

If several of these capabilities are missing, the organization may have deployed a model, but it does not yet have a mature MLOps capability.

Final Thoughts

MLOps is the operating discipline that separates an AI demo from an AI system an enterprise can depend on.

Models encounter new data. User behavior changes. Infrastructure fails. Model providers update. Prompts evolve. Knowledge bases become stale. Agents gain access to more tools.

The right response is a continuous lifecycle:

Build → Evaluate → Deploy → Monitor → Diagnose → Improve → Re-evaluate

At SotaTek, we treat MLOps, LLMOps, and AI operations as part of the production architecture, connecting model evaluation, versioning, monitoring, integration, and operational controls rather than adding monitoring as an afterthought.

The best MLOps teams are not necessarily the teams that retrain models most often. They are the teams that know when behavior changed, why it changed, whether it matters, and what action should follow.

For a deeper look at the monitoring framework, production lifecycle, and enterprise implementation approach, read our AI MLOps and Monitoring guide.

oneSentenceSummary: 文章指出，部署模型不等于运营 AI 系统，并提出一套全面的 MLOps 反馈闭环：对所有组件进行版本管理、监控多种信号，并将遥测数据转化为运营行动，以提升生产环境 AI 的可靠性。
summary: 本文阐释了机器学习模型在生产环境中的成功，取决于远不止模型监控。文章提出一种整体性的 MLOps 方法，将 AI 运维视为持续性的工程实践。现代 AI 系统，尤其是 LLM 应用和智能体，不仅需要对模型检查点进行版本管理，还需要管理提示词、嵌入向量、检索配置和防护机制的版本。文章介绍了涵盖实验跟踪、CI/CD、持续训练和回滚能力的生产生命周期，并区分了数据质量问题、训练与服务偏差、数据漂移、预测漂移和概念漂移等不同故障信号，强调仅检测漂移并不足够。对于 LLM 应用，文章建议分别监控检索层和生成层；对于 AI 智能体，则必须监控其执行轨迹。最后，文章给出一份涵盖版本管理、评估、监控和事件响应的实用清单，确保 AI 系统能够实现业务成果，而不只是保持技术层面的健康。

mainPoints.point: MLOps 不仅限于模型监控，还涵盖整个 AI 系统生命周期
mainPoints.explanation: 生产环境中的 MLOps 系统必须打通实验、数据管道、模型训练、评估、部署、监控和事件响应，以便回答有关模型版本、输入分布变化和业务影响等关键问题。

mainPoints.point: 生成式 AI 将运维范围扩展到了模型制品之外
mainPoints.explanation: LLM 应用依赖基础模型、系统提示词、上下文窗口、嵌入向量、RAG 配置、防护机制、工具定义和智能体工作流；诊断性能退化时，这些组件都必须进行版本管理和追踪。

mainPoints.point: 检测漂移后，应先进行诊断，再决定是否触发重新训练
mainPoints.explanation: 分布变化只能说明发生了变化，并不能证明重新训练就能解决问题。结构化的响应流程应先验证数据质量、衡量对模型的实际影响并分析根本原因，再决定是回滚、重新训练还是修复管道。

mainPoints.point: LLM 和智能体监控需要覆盖多个层面的专用遥测数据
mainPoints.explanation: 要有效管理生产环境中的 AI 系统，传统 ML 监控还必须纳入答案正确性、依据充分性、幻觉、检索召回率、工具选择准确率、权限违规情况，以及每项已完成任务的成本等信号。

mainPoints.point: 生产事件应转化为回归测试，推动后续版本改进
mainPoints.explanation: 反馈闭环应记录生产环境中的故障、据此创建新的评估用例并添加回归测试，让评估数据集成为生产经验的记录，从而持续提升系统可靠性。

keyQuotes: 「机器学习模型即使在评估中表现出色，仍可能在生产环境中失败。」
「这就是为什么部署模型不等于运营 AI 系统。」
「目标不只是发现问题，而是明确下一步该采取什么工程行动。」
「监控会告诉你出了问题，可观测性则能帮助你了解原因。」
